rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the six-peak elution window and identify critical pairs while limiting late-elution risk. A midrange temperature leaves room to tune selectivity in either direction.
The first method already reaches the maximum CRF. Shorten the gradient by one grid step to seek a faster fully resolved method while testing the critical pair’s sensitivity to slope.

Injection 2 retains the maximum CRF with a shorter run, but its critical pair is near the resolution threshold. Raise temperature one step to test whether selectivity permits further acceleration without losing full resolution.
The temperature increase improved the critical pair while preserving maximum CRF. Shorten the gradient one step to establish whether that selectivity gain supports a faster fully resolved separation.

Narrow the solvent window to restore approximately the successful eight-minute gradient’s slope while reducing the initial low-organic segment. This should recover critical-pair resolution and potentially finish sooner than injection 3.
Raise both endpoints by one step to retain the successful gradient slope while removing more low-organic time. The first peak remains sufficiently retained to justify testing this faster window.

Increase the starting organic fraction to shorten retention, keeping the endpoint fixed for a slightly shallower gradient. That slope adjustment may preserve critical-pair resolution as the elution window moves earlier.
Raise temperature one step to shorten the current fastest fully resolved method. Earlier temperature testing improved the critical middle pair, while the other pairs currently have resolution margin.

Move the starting composition higher to reduce retention, while making the gradient shallower to protect the critical middle pair. This tests whether a narrower solvent window can retain maximum CRF in a faster separation.

Trim the endpoint above the last peak’s estimated elution composition of 0.49 and shorten the gradient to four minutes. The resulting slope is only slightly steeper than injection 9, offering a faster separation with a reasonable chance of preserving full resolution.

Test a substantially steeper gradient at lower temperature to see whether the critical middle pair separates again after an elution-order reversal. This exploratory run could reveal a faster fully resolved regime, while injection 10 remains the fastest validated maximum-CRF method.

Test a steeper gradient and lower temperature to seek separation on the opposite side of the middle-pair crossover. Lowering the starting organic fraction protects early-peak retention while exploring this potentially faster regime.

Return to the successful moderate-slope regime and test a higher starting composition for faster elution. Lowering temperature should protect early-pair separation, while the shallower slope may compensate for reduced middle-pair resolution.

Return to injection 8’s starting composition and temperature, increasing only the endpoint to accelerate elution. Its middle-pair resolution of 1.85 provides some margin for this modest slope increase, potentially matching or improving injection 10’s time.

Test a small slope increase from the fastest fully resolved method, injection 10, using a six-minute gradient to access an intermediate grid slope. This probes whether its remaining resolution margin permits a further reduction in last-peak time.

Test whether another temperature step improves the middle pair enough to permit faster separation than injection 10. The early pair may become limiting, so this run establishes the upper-temperature boundary rather than assuming full resolution.

Explore a colder, higher-starting-organic regime that may change middle-pair selectivity while retaining the early compounds. This tests an alternative route to a faster separation; injection 10 remains the fastest validated maximum-CRF method.

Refine the cold, high-organic regime by raising the start and reducing the slope, testing whether the middle-pair separation grows. The early pair had substantial resolution margin in injection 17, but its compression will need monitoring.

Keep the starting composition fixed and reduce the slope to isolate its effect on the remaining critical pair. This tests whether the cold regime can reach full resolution near a two-minute last-peak time without further compressing the early peaks.

Test a much shallower gradient in the cold regime to determine whether the middle pair can reach full resolution without raising the starting organic fraction. The lower endpoint should still elute the last compound comfortably within the acquisition window.

Return to the high-temperature regime, lowering the starting organic fraction to recover the early-pair resolution lost in injection 16. A moderate slope should preserve middle-pair separation while testing another compact, fully resolved method.

Return to 50 C and test a small slope increase over injection 14 using a shorter programmed gradient. This probes the resolution boundary for a last-peak time potentially below injection 10’s 3.40 minutes.

Test whether a higher starting composition in the cold regime can lift the middle pair above 1.5, since changing slope alone had little effect. This is a boundary test with a risk of compressing the early pair; injection 10 remains the fastest validated maximum-CRF method.

Back off the slope near the fastest validated method to increase resolution margin while retaining a short separation. With maximum CRF already achieved, this run seeks a less borderline alternative to injection 10.

Preserve injection 24’s successful starting composition, temperature, and gradient slope while trimming the endpoint and programmed duration. All peaks should elute before the gradient ends, retaining maximum CRF and its resolution margin in a shorter programmed method.
